subject: history
title: Company Raj: From Plassey to Crown Rule
welcome_lead: Trace how a trading company became a territorial sovereign and why the 1857 Rebellion ended Company rule.
meta_desc: A-Level History adventure on the British Empire in India: Plassey 1757, East India Company rule, the 1857 Rebellion and the 1858 transfer to Crown rule.
final_note: You now grasp the shift from commerce to conquest and the constitutional transformation of 1858.

concepts.def: Robert Clive's victory over Siraj-ud-Daulah of Bengal, securing East India Company dominance in Bengal and marking the start of territorial empire.
Chartered English trading company (1600) that acquired diwani rights in 1765 and governed vast Indian territories until 1858.
Right to collect revenue in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa granted by Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II, giving the Company fiscal sovereignty.
Annexation policy under Dalhousie (1848-56) absorbing princely states without natural male heirs, fuelling resentment.
Major uprising sparked by sepoy grievances (greased cartridges) that spread across northern India and prompted the abolition of Company rule.
Statute transferring EIC powers to the Crown, creating the Secretary of State for India and ending Company government.

walkthroughs.body_html: Plassey (23 June 1757) was less a battle than a coup: Clive bribed Mir Jafar to defect, defeating Siraj-ud-Daulah. Buxar (1764) confirmed Company supremacy and led to the Diwani grant of 1765, by which the Mughal emperor licensed Company revenue collection. The result was a hybrid: nominal Mughal sovereignty, real Company power. Regulating Act 1773 and Pitt's India Act 1784 imposed parliamentary oversight via the Board of Control.

Long-term causes included annexations under the Doctrine of Lapse (Jhansi, Satara, Nagpur), the displacement of Awadh in 1856, evangelical missionary activity and resentment at Westernising reforms. The immediate trigger was the Enfield rifle cartridge, rumoured to be greased with cow and pig fat, offending Hindu and Muslim sepoys alike. Mutiny at Meerut (10 May 1857) cascaded into a wider rebellion centred on Delhi, Lucknow and Kanpur.

After brutal reconquest, the Government of India Act 1858 abolished the EIC, vesting authority in the Crown via a Secretary of State and a 15-member Council of India. Queen Victoria's Proclamation promised religious toleration and respect for princely treaties. The Viceroy replaced the Governor-General as Crown representative. This formalised the British Raj that would last until 1947.
